book: 288 - Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas

chapters.relation: In this foreword Joshua Wolf Shenk recounts an intoxicating blind date with 'Rachael' to argue that dating exposes the core existential dilemma of social creatures: we crave ecstasy (ekstasis, 'standing outside oneself') yet can only connect by holding on to a discrete identity. He blames the modern isolation of the self on Descartes' claim that the self inhabits its own subjective realm and Hobbes' picture of natural man as solitary, and cites Camus that once you choose to live, the real question is how to relate to others. His unresolved paradox—needing the mantra 'I was complete before I met you' while knowing it is false—frames love as the tension between self-sufficiency and merger.

Editors Kristie Miller and Marlene Clark introduce the volume by opening with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics claim that the human drive to couple is even stronger than the drive to live as a political being and that fulfillment rests in loving relationships. They frame dating as a rule-governed 'game' with aims and strategies and preview each contributor's essay—Jenkins on flirting, Langan on conservative men, Samp and Cohen against unconditional love, the elevator metaphor, cyberdating, evolutionary seduction, and Colyvan's game-theoretic mate search—tying age-old ethical questions about treating partners well to new work in evolutionary psychology, decision theory, and the ethics of online romance.

Carrie Jenkins does analytic conceptual analysis of flirting, rejecting the Oxford English Dictionary's claim that flirting requires having no serious intentions. She distinguishes 'flirting' from merely 'behaving flirtatiously' (Joe who over-holds eye contact, the tourist touching her earlobe in Italy are flirtatious without flirting) and argues flirting requires an intention to act in ways disposed to raise flirter-flirtee romance to salience, done in a 'knowing yet playful' way. Borrowing Kripke's 'killer yellow' to imagine 'killer-flirts' who die on contact, and citing chatbot studies, she concludes one can flirt with an imagined or non-human target only if one believes it can respond significantly.

Emily Langan uses focus-group data from 75 self-described ideologically conservative, mostly Christian young men to argue that flirting is a site of moral decision-making, opening with Hitch's 'right broom' line to show these men reject its libido-driven premise. She reports three shared themes—flirting is not about sex but about honesty of motive, timing within a relationship's stages, and reciprocity ('it has to be a two-way street')—and three tensions (healthy vs. harmful, superficial vs. serious, overt vs. covert), drawing on courtship-stage and flirting-style research to show that, contrary to the stereotype that only women agonize over relationships, conservative men wrestle with being 'risqué yet respectable.'

Jennifer Samp and Andrew Cohen argue against the Notebook-style romantic ideal of unconditional love, casting dating as a 'calculated exchange' explained by social-exchange and interdependence theory (comparison level and comparison level of alternatives). Adopting Aristotle's distinction between friendships of utility/pleasure and 'complete friendships' in which one values the friend as 'another self' and as an end in itself, they hold the best romances are complete friendships—yet insist even these must be conditioned. Their key thought experiment: a genuinely boundless love would survive discovering one's partner is a child-molesting murderer; since it should not, 'true love knows bounds' and remains part of a good life only because it can be defeated by such reasons.

John Rowan and Patricia Hallen build an extended elevator metaphor for dating (Ann and Bob riding floors, pushing buttons to raise or lower intimacy, gravity pulling toward breakup) to capture Heraclitus's insight that a relationship is a reality in constant change, while invoking Plato to insist the conceptual reality of a relationship is as real as physical objects. They define dating as gauging the possibility of eventual commitment, cite Hume's canoe image for implicit communication of shared destination, and ground their strategies—be yourself, go slowly, communicate, befriend—in Aristotle's virtue ethics, treating honesty, courage, and loyalty as habits lying in the golden mean between deficiency and excess (e.g., the Look Who's Talking date who overshares is 'excessively honest').

Mary Beth Yount asks whether being 'crazy in love' really resembles mental illness, noting lovesickness was a diagnosis for nearly two millennia and that love's mood swings mimic bipolar or schizophrenic symptoms. She organizes the analysis around the four Greek loves—eros (with Plato's ladder from physical beauty to the Forms, i.e., 'Platonic love'), philia (Aristotle's Nicomachean friendship of good character), storge (familial affection), and agape (C.S. Lewis's unconditional charity)—arguing a full romance blends all four. She then surveys Fisher, Aron, and Brown's fMRI work showing romantic love as a dopamine-driven mammalian mate-choice drive stronger than the sex drive, and the 'protest'/'resignation' stages of rejection, to reassure daters their craziness is normal biology, not disorder.

Kristie Miller asks whether any dating behavior—dating a sibling, a gorilla, or a blow-up doll—is genuinely 'taboo' in the prudential (self-interested, utility-maximizing) rather than ethical sense, using decision theory's notion of maximizing expected utility. She sorts behaviors labeled 'pathological' into merely conventionally pathological, pseudo-pathological (e.g., polyandry explained by resource scarcity and childrearing), and genuinely pathological (arising from malfunctioning evolved mate-selection modules like symmetry or MHC-odor detection). Because inclusive fitness and utility diverge, and using future-selves discounting and weakness of will (the stable partner vs. the bad-boy biker), she concludes that in some circumstances even dating a sibling or a gorilla can be the utility-maximizing, and thus rational, choice.

Anne Barnhill uses John Cusack's boom-box serenade in Say Anything, his poolside pleading in The Sure Thing, and Andy Bernard's 'Take a Chance on Me' serenade in The Office to defend 'prospective boundary violation'—violating a boundary that would not exist in a closer relationship in order to create that relationship. She rejects the Kantian reading of Korsgaard and Hill that treating people as ends forbids all non-rational manipulation, arguing instead that such charming pushiness is 'faking it till you make it,' which works via Aristotle's habituation whereby feelings catch up with actions. She then sets four rules (no harm, not too much closer too fast, genuinely wanting the relationship, and that the other would plausibly want it) to separate appropriate from wrong boundary violations.

Kyla Reid and Tinashe Dune attack the bestselling dating manual The Rules by Fein and Schneider, focusing on Rule 4 (never go Dutch—let the man pay) and Rule 12 (dump him if he gives no romantic gift like jewelry). They line up 'Rules Girls' against sex workers offering a paid 'girlfriend experience' and 'professional girlfriends'/gold diggers, arguing that all three approach relationships in a systematic, 'business-like' way that packages and markets the woman as a product, measures her worth by what the man spends, and treats gifts like performance bonuses. Because monogamy, public recognition, and belief in the relationship cannot make it authentic, they conclude The Rules obstruct genuine intimacy and that everyone should be more critical of dating conventions about who pays and what gifts mean.

Joshua Heter mounts a virtue-theoretic case against being set up on blind dates, using Aristotle's notion of telos and the distinction between fleeting 'hot-fudge happiness' and eudaimonia, the flourishing of a well-lived life (illustrated by long-married Bill and Fran). He argues a 'guy's' function is achieved by exercising his whole nature, and dramatizes this with Zoo-bear versus Wild-bear: the zoo-fed bear has its hunger and safety met but cannot flourish because it never hunts or roams, just as matchmaking meets the romantic need while letting a man's 'social muscles' atrophy. Invoking Aristotle's philia (and Nussbaum on Aristotelian virtue), he concedes friends mean well but recommends they merely introduce people and let things progress naturally rather than force an 'unnatural' match.
